title: Turned box bag — gusset ring, zipper panel, seams inside
summary: Two flat panels and a gusset ring, sewn RIGHT SIDES TOGETHER with a {sa} seam allowance and turned right side out through the zip. The allowances finish inside, the finished edge is the stitch line, and the cut pieces are the finished size plus an allowance all round. This is the ordinary way a bag of this kind is made; nothing here is unusual, and that is the point.

docs.title: A zipped pocket built into a panel

assembly.title: Pre-wash and dry the shell
assembly.body: A natural-fibre shell shrinks; wash and dry it the way the finished bag will be washed, before a single piece is cut. A synthetic one does not, and this step does not apply to it.

assembly.title: Test on scrap before you cut anything
assembly.body:
Sew two scraps together with a {sa} allowance, turn them, and look at the seam. You are checking three things: that the machine drives the stack, that {sa} comes out where you think it does against your foot or guide, and that the seam turns and sits flat. Everything in this pattern is measured from the stitch line, so a run that drifts an eighth is an eighth off every dimension.

While you are there, curve a corner on the scrap, clip it, and turn it. That is the only operation here that takes practice.

figures.caption: The seam you are testing, in section: two pieces face to face, allowance inside, and the finished edge is the stitching itself.

assembly.title: Cut, and leave the gusset long
assembly.body:
Every piece is cut FINISHED SIZE PLUS {sa} ON EVERY EDGE — the ordinary rule, and the reason a {w} wide bag is cut from a {panel_w} panel.

Rotary-cut against a straightedge. The shell is polyester and does not ravel, so no edge needs turning under and nothing needs sealing; a lighter tidies a cut end if you want it neat, and that is all. Clips hold better than pins on a coated face and do not leave holes, but this is an ordinary water-resistant canvas, not a technical laminate — a pin where it will end up inside a seam allowance is not a problem.

Cut the gusset at {gusset_cut_long} rather than its finished {gusset_cut} and leave it long until the ring is fitted. Cut long, fit, then trim: the ring's true length depends on the allowance you actually achieve.

Any piece carrying embroidery is cut OVERSIZED and trimmed to size after the machine is done with it. Cut the rounded corners round a template rather than by eye — the panels and the outer lower pieces share that curve, and two corners that disagree show up as a pucker.

figures.caption: Cut long and trimmed later — the offcut you lose once the ring is fitted.

assembly.title: Finish the inside allowances
assembly.body:
Turned, the allowances finish INSIDE where nothing wears them — but a shell that ravels will still shed into the bag over its life. Zigzag or overlock the long edges of the panels and the gusset before assembly, while everything is still flat.

A shell that does not ravel skips this entirely, which is most of why the family prefers one.

assembly.title: Embroider now, flat, before anything is assembled
assembly.body:
Any piece that carries a design has to be stitched flat, before anything is behind it. Design to 96 mm or less — this machine's field is 100 × 100 mm.

Most of these pieces are too small to hoop: the frame needs fabric well past its window on every side to clamp. The answer is the usual one — embroider an OVERSIZED BLANK floated on sticky-back tear-away that is hooped by itself, baste it down, and cut the piece out of the blank afterwards. The Operation Manual describes the float on p.64.

Keep the design {seam_margin} clear of every finished edge so it is not stitched into a seam allowance.

figures.caption: Every face that carries a design, each a separate hooping, all before assembly.

assembly.title: Lay the chain the right way up
assembly.body:
**Standard coil**, so the spiral is meant to be seen: lay the chain coil-UP, facing you, and bring the shell onto the tape either side of it.

Check before the first row. Close the zip, set it on the bench the way the bag will hang, and look — you should see the spiral and the pull. There is no undo: build it the other way up and the finished bag has its pull on the inside.

assembly.title: Lay the chain the right way up
assembly.body:
**Reverse coil**, so the outside shows flat tape: lay the chain coil-DOWN and bring the shell onto the tape from above.

Check before the first row. Close the zip, set it on the bench the way the bag will hang, and look — if you can see the spiral, turn it over. There is no undo: build it the other way up and the finished bag has its pull on the inside. A reverse slider is a different part from a standard one.

assembly.title: Chassis webbing onto the gusset INTERIOR
assembly.body:
A bag carried by straps needs a webbing loop round its girth so the load pulls on webbing rather than on cloth. Topstitch it down both edges along the gusset's inside face, keeping it clear of the centreline where the coil will sit.

Do it now, while the gusset is flat.

figures.caption: The tack itself, in the order it is sewn.

assembly.title: Build the zipper panel
assembly.stitch: straight, {lap} then topstitch, 3.0 mm, zipper foot
assembly.body:
The standard install, and the reason nothing raw shows on the finished bag: the strip is sewn to the tape FACE DOWN and then folded back off the coil, so its raw edge finishes between the strip and the tape.

Lay the {strip_front} strip face down on the zip with its raw edge along the tape, sew {lap} from that edge with a zipper foot, then fold the strip back away from the coil and topstitch through the fold. Repeat with the {strip_rear} strip on the other side. Basting tape holds it while you sew.

**Sew both strips in the same direction.** Sewing the second one back the other way bows the panel: the tape feeds slightly differently under the foot each way.

About {reveal} of tape shows beside the coil on each side once the strips are folded back. That is deliberate — the fold has to clear the coil or the foot rides up on it — and it is counted in the width: the panel finishes {gusset_w} across, matching the gusset it is about to join.

The panel is cut {zip_cut} long: {zip_face} of opening plus {sa} at each end for the seams that close the ring.

figures.caption: The panel at its own strip widths, and the finished width it has to match.

assembly.title: Shorten the zipper and make a new stop
assembly.stitch: dense zigzag ~3 mm wide at 0.4 mm, 5–6 passes
assembly.body:
Open it halfway so the slider is well clear, then work a dense zigzag back and forth across the coil at the new length — this machine has no programmed bar-tack. Trim 1" beyond the tack, never flush, and cap the cut end with a scrap.

A coil zipper cut without a new stop lets the slider run straight off the end, and there is no putting it back on in a hurry.

figures.caption: Tack first, trim 1" beyond it, then cap.

assembly.title: Ring anchors onto the gusset interior
assembly.body:
Each D-ring needs something behind it, or the bag hangs off two stitch fields in one layer of shell. Lay a {ring_anchor_len} × {ring_anchor_w} strip across the gusset's inside face at each ring position, running its full cut width so both ends finish inside the seam allowances. Topstitch both long edges.

Do it now, while the gusset is a flat strip and the positions are fixed.

figures.caption: Topstitched along both long edges, while the gusset is still flat.

assembly.title: D-ring tabs, from the outside
assembly.body: Fold a 4" tab of webbing through each D-ring and box-X it to the gusset's OUTSIDE — the face that will end up outward — over the anchor strip behind. Do it now, while the gusset is still a flat strip: the same reason the anchors went on first. The tack goes through tab, gusset and anchor at once — the thickest stack on the bag, so hand-wheel it.

figures.caption: Where the rings land. The tack goes through tab, gusset and anchor at once.

assembly.title: Close the ring
assembly.body:
Both joins are plain seams, sewn RIGHT SIDES TOGETHER at {sa} — the same seam as everywhere else on this bag, and the allowances finish inside.

Trim the gusset first: target {gusset_cut}, which is {gusset_face} of finished ring plus {sa} at each end. Then seam each end of the gusset to an end of the zipper panel. Press the allowances toward the gusset, or finger-press and topstitch them down if you want them to stay put.

The ring now measures {ring} at the stitch line, which is the finished perimeter of a panel.

**Mark the ring's four quarter points before you go any further** — the two joins, the midpoint of the zip and the midpoint of the base. Matching those to the panel is what stops the ring wandering as you sew it on.

figures.caption: Closed. Mark the quarter points now — matching them to the panel is what keeps the ring from twisting.

assembly.title: Close the chassis loop across the top face
assembly.body: Overlap the webbing's ends across the top face, clear of the coil, and box-X the overlap. That closes the loop the whole bag hangs from.

figures.caption: Where the loop closes, clear of the coil.

assembly.title: Grab handle
assembly.body: Box-X both ends of the handle to the gusset, through the webbing behind it. Same tack as the D-ring tabs and the same thickness.

assembly.title: Pockets onto the gusset, over the webbing
assembly.body: An applied pocket goes on the gusset's inside face, over the webbing, while the gusset is flat. Its top edge is hemmed; its other three sides finish inside the panel seams.

assembly.title: Pocketed panel, zip ACROSS — two layers, pocket between them
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot
assembly.body:
A panel that carries a pocket is two pieces, not one, and nothing is cut open. The OUTER layer is split: set the {top_upper} upper and the {top_lower} lower onto the pocket zipper the same way you did the zipper panel — face down, sewn {lap} from the raw edge, folded back off the coil and topstitched through the fold. Reassembled it measures {panel_h} — the same as the inner.

The INNER layer is a full {panel_w} × {panel_h} panel. Lay the outer over it, wrong sides together, baste round the edge inside the seam allowance, and from here treat the pair as ONE panel. The pocket is the cavity between them; the zip is its only mouth.

Shorten the zip and bar-tack a stop just inside the seam line at each end — those ends finish inside the seam.

figures.caption: The inner layer is the compartment wall; the pocket is the cavity in front of it.

assembly.title: Pocketed panel, zip DOWN — two layers, pocket between them
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot
assembly.body:
Same sandwich, turned. The OUTER layer splits into a NEAR piece {side_near} wide and a FAR piece {side_far} wide, both {side_across} tall, set onto the tape the same way as the zipper panel: face down, sewn {lap} from the raw edge, folded back and topstitched through the fold. Reassembled it measures {panel_w}.

The INNER layer is a full {panel_w} × {panel_h} panel. Lay the outer over it, wrong sides together, baste inside the seam allowance, and treat the pair as one panel.

The zip sits {side_zip} in from the panel's cut edge and does not run the whole way: it starts {side_starts} down and runs {side_run}. Above that the two outer pieces lap onto EACH OTHER rather than onto tape — same lap, same two rows, one continuous line — so only the zipper is short. Bar-tack a stop at the top of the run.

A vertical opening keeps both outer pieces caught in the panel seam along their own outside edge, where a horizontal one leaves the lower piece hanging from the zipper alone.

figures.caption: On the panel: the run is vertical and stops short of the top.

assembly.title: Placket over the pocket zip
assembly.stitch: caught in the lap's two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot
assembly.body:
The flap that hides the zip. Lay the {side_placket_long} × {side_placket} placket over the NEAR piece with its edge level, so {lap} of it is caught in the two rows that lap that piece onto the tape and {side_placket_show} hangs free across the coil.

It is caught in a seam you are sewing anyway: no new seam, one more cut piece. Its free edge is left raw — the shell does not ravel, and a hem there would stiffen the one thing the flap has to stay, which is limp enough to lie flat over a coil.

figures.caption: The flap, over the coil, on the face that goes against the body.

assembly.title: Divider pocket onto the {divider_face} panel
assembly.stitch: hem 3.0 mm; channels straight at 3.0 mm
assembly.body:
Hem the divider's TOP edge — turn {sa} once to the wrong side and topstitch. That is the only edge of it that gets a finish of its own; the other three finish inside the panel seam.

Lay it on the INTERIOR of the {divider_face} panel with its sides and bottom flush to the panel's raw edges and baste inside the seam allowance. Topstitch the channel lines from the divider side, through divider and panel.

It finishes {divider_depth} deep with {divider_clear} of open panel above it.

figures.caption: Cut to the panel, so its sides and bottom finish inside the panel's own seam. Only its top edge is hemmed.

assembly.title: Belt keepers, and the anchor behind them
assembly.body: A single-layer back panel has nothing behind the keeper, so it gets an anchor strip: lay it across the panel's inside face at the keeper line, then box-X each keeper end through keeper, panel and anchor at once.

assembly.title: Belt keepers, through both layers of the back panel
assembly.body:
Fold each {keeper_w} × {keeper_len} keeper around a scrap of the actual belt to get the tunnel right, then box-X both ends through keeper and panel. Both ends — one tack per keeper is not enough.

Do it before the panel goes into the ring, while it is flat.

figures.caption: Both tacks sit above the zip, so neither crosses the pocket.
Why above: there the box-X reaches the inner layer.

assembly.title: Build the back panel — applied pockets and ribs
assembly.body: Hem the top edge of each applied pocket, lay it on the panel, and topstitch its sides and bottom. A divider rib is topstitched down both long edges. Everything applied goes on while the panel is flat.

assembly.title: Belt keeper onto the back panel
assembly.body:
Fold the {keeper_w} × {keeper_len} keeper round a scrap of the actual belt to get the tunnel right, then box-X both ends to the panel. Both ends.

Do it while the panel is flat.

assembly.title: Back panel into the ring
assembly.body:
**Right sides together.** Lay the ring on the panel, right sides facing, and pin with all raw edges level — the ring's outer edge on the panel's outer edge, right the way round. Match the ring's quarter marks to the panel's — the two ring seams to the top corners, the zip's midpoint to the top centre, the gusset's midpoint to the base — then fill in between. Matching centres first and working outward is what stops the ring wandering.

Sew with the GUSSET underneath and the panel on top, so you can see the panel's curve and follow it; the feed dogs ease the slight fullness of the lower layer round the corner for you.

At each rounded corner the gusset's raw edge has to reach further than its stitch line. Clip it: {relief_clips} snips per curve, each cut to {clip_depth} — an eighth SHORT of the stitch line. Never cut to the line; the stitching pulls out of it.

Trim the allowance back to about ¼" through the corners once it is sewn, to keep the bulk down when it turns.

figures.caption: Right sides together, all raw edges level, allowance to the outside — it folds inside when the bag is turned.

assembly.title: Front panel — open the zipper FIRST
assembly.body:
**Open the zip before you sew this seam.** It is the only way back into the bag: everything is enclosed after this, and the zip is what you turn the whole thing through.

Then the same again — right sides together, quarter marks matched, gusset underneath, clipped and trimmed at the curves. Take it slowly at the two lap joins, where the ring is thickest.

This is the last chance to look inside.

figures.caption: THE zipper — the main one, on the top face. Open it before this seam: it is what you turn the bag through.

assembly.title: Turn it, and work the corners out
assembly.body:
Reach in through the open zip, take hold of the far side, and pull the bag through itself. It comes out stiff and creased — that is normal.

The seam allowance is folded inside now, and the corners are where it is thickest — that is why it was trimmed. Work each corner out from the inside with a blunt point: the eraser end of a pencil, a chopstick, a point turner. Never anything sharp, and never force it — the seam is what gives.

Then persuade the seams to sit. On this cloth **finger-press and roll the seam between your fingers rather than reaching for the iron.** If you do press, use LOW heat, a press cloth, and keep moving — a coated polyester will glaze or shrink under a hot iron. Test on the scrap from step 1 first. Stuffing the bag and leaving it a day does most of the work on its own.

figures.caption: What the seam becomes: the allowance folds inside and the stitching is the finished edge.

assembly.title: Straps, belt and hardware
assembly.body: Thread the strap through its hardware and clip it to the D-rings.

assembly.title: Base stiffener, loose
assembly.body: Cut it to the FLOOR, not to the face — on a rounded-bottom bag the flat floor is two radii shorter. It drops in loose so it can come out to wash the bag.

assembly.title: Thread your belt, clip your strap
assembly.body: Nothing left to sew. Slide your belt through both keepers and check it runs without binding — if the tunnel is tight, unpick ONE tack, refit the keeper round the actual belt, re-tack and trim. The strap clips to the two D-rings with its own hooks.

figures.caption: Nothing left to sew.
